system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms (for example rates by inhibitor level, dose-normalised concentrations, effect against concentration over time).
3. Retrieve: search the mechanism library and read the relevant cards. They give equations, data signatures, pitfalls and the library model name to fit.
4. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
5. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
6. Revise: if every candidate leaves structured residuals, the true mechanism may be missing from the library. Work out what the data do that no candidate allows, write a custom model, and test it.
7. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
8. Submit with submit_model, citing fit_ids (and card ids you read) as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 16 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates within the measured substrate range.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

content.thinking:
The substrate inhibition term drops out here, since the inhibition constant is so large that the model reduces to plain Michaelis-Menten, and the Hill coefficient near 1 supports that. The data look close to linear, with v/S holding around 0.2 across the range and perhaps a slight dip at high substrate, so I'm treating the fit as effectively v = kS with k near 0.2 (

I'm checking whether the intercept matters, since the linear fit's 0.036 looks like noise at low substrate. The one-parameter linear model is the simpler candidate next to the two-parameter Michaelis-Menten fit, and I'm fitting it to compare BIC.

content.text: The substrate-inhibition fit collapses to the MM limit (Ksi → very large), and the Hill exponent is ~1.1. The data look almost linear in S (v/S ≈ 0.2 throughout), so I'll test the one-parameter linear model.

content.thinking:
I'm comparing the linear and Michaelis-Menten fits: the MM model has a BIC about 3.1 lower, which favors it by roughly 4.7 times, and its residual sigma drops from 0.101 to 0.087. Within the measured range the two models give nearly the same predictions, so the question is which one to submit. Since MM is the mechanistic model and BIC supports it, I'm leaning toward submitting MM and noting the Vmax

I'm noting that Km can't be pinned down separately from Vmax, but the prediction within the measured range is still reliable, and my confidence in this choice is moderate.

input.summary: Single-substrate Michaelis-Menten kinetics (fit1: Vmax≈34.5, Km≈160 uM, additive error, no residual structure, BIC -74.6). Substrate inhibition collapsed to the MM limit (fit3, Ksi→∞), so there is no evidence of high-substrate decline. Hill cooperativity gave n≈1.11 with poorly determined K and worse BIC (fit2, -73.4). A one-parameter linear rate (fit4, BIC -71.5, residual sigma 0.101 vs 0.087) fits nearly as well within the measured range, so the data are mostly in the first-order regime (S << Km). Vmax and Km are not separately identifiable; only Vmax/Km ≈ 0.22 uM/min/uM is well determined, and predictions within 0.5–20 uM are what matter.
